cases.title: `fill<u32, N>(0)` emits `0.0` elements, and Tint refuses the WGSL
cases.body:
## What happens

`fill<T, N>(v)` builds an `array<T, N>` with every element `v`. It does not type `v` to `T`. A bare `0` is an `f32` on this surface, so `fill<u32, 4>(0)` builds an `array<u32, 4>` of `f32` literals:

```ts
'use typeshade';
export function walk(n: u32): u32 {
  let s: array<u32, 4> = fill<u32, 4>(0);
  s[0] = n;
  return s[0];
}
```

`compile()` reports no diagnostic and emits:

```wgsl
var s: array<u32, 4> = array<u32, 4>(0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0);
```

Tint (Chromium 141.0.7390.37, SwiftShader) refuses it:

```text
error: cannot convert value of type 'abstract-float' to type 'u32'
```

So a program `compile()` accepts does not run. Found while writing proposal 0047 (#495, PR #496).

## Why

`lowerFill` in `src/compiler/ts/lower/expression-array.ts` lowers the value with no expected type and passes it to `fillArray` as it is. `array<T, N>(…)` types each element with `typeArrayElement`, which retargets an integer literal and refuses a value of another type. `fill` skips that step.

## What was expected

`fill<u32, 4>(0)` emits `array<u32, 4>(0u, 0u, 0u, 0u)`, as `array<u32, 4>(0, 0, 0, 0)` does. A value of another type is refused with the element message the list form gives (Rule 12.5), for example `fill<u32, 4>(1.5)`.

## Rules

Rule 1.3 (a program the compiler accepts runs on the target) and Rule 11.3 (the emitted text satisfies Tint).

## Tests owed

- `fill<u32, 4>(0)`, `fill<i32, 3>(-1)` and `fill<vec2, 2>(vec2(1., 2.))` emit typed elements on WGSL and GLSL ES 3.00, and both CPU paths read them.
- `fill<u32, 4>(1.5)` is refused with code and text.

## Pinned commit

- `main` at c57fbdc (`c57fbdc9c99a33d12fb2616bd2a832f638f113ad`), measured 2026-10-05 in bun 1.3.14.

cases.title: GLSL: a literal index into a storage array of vectors or structs fails the emit with "i32 * u32"
cases.body:
## What happens

In a fragment entry, a storage array whose element takes more than one word, read at an integer literal index, has no GLSL. `compile()` gives WGSL, but the GLSL ES 3.00 emit fails its own module validation, and the author gets a `TS8015` warning in the compiler's internal words:

```ts
"use typeshade";
class L { a: vec4; b: vec4; }
declare const ls: storage<array<L>>;
@fragment
export function fs(): vec4 { return ls[1].b; }
```

```text
TS8015 Backend emit failed: typeshade [SD0020]: module validation failed (4 errors):
  - mixed-scalar (fn fs): mixed-scalar binop in fn 'fs': i32 * u32 — WGSL has no implicit int/float conversion
```

| Read | GLSL |
| --- | --- |
| `xs[0]` on `storage<array<f32>>` | emitted |
| `vs[i]` on `storage<array<vec4>>`, `const i = u32(1)` | emitted |
| `ls[i].b` on `storage<array<L>>`, `const i = u32(0)` | emitted |
| `vs[0]` on `storage<array<vec4>>` | fails, `i32 * u32` |
| `ls[1].b` on `storage<array<L>>` | fails, `i32 * u32` |

The storage emulation seems to multiply the index by the element's word stride. A literal index is an `i32` there, and the stride a `u32`. A `u32` index and a one-word element both avoid the mixed product.

## Expected

The literal index is converted to the stride's type, as a `u32` variable already is, and the module has GLSL with no diagnostic.

## Found by

The engine journey (proposal 0025, step 5). It reads its two lights from a uniform struct instead of indexing a storage array, so it does not depend on this fix.

## Tests owed

The GLSL emit of `vs[0]` and `ls[1].b` in a fragment entry, linked on a WebGL2 context by the compile gate, and the CPU and WebGPU values against WebGL2's.

tshc on Windows: every path resolves to "/D:/...", so check and sync find no file
cases.body:
## What happens

On Windows, `tshc check` and `tshc sync` stop before they read a file:

```
PS D:\stepinside> bun vendor/typeshade/src/cli/bin.ts check src/
tshc: no file or directory at src/.
```

The exit status is 2, and `sync` fails the same way, so a host whose `build` script runs `tshc sync` (typeshade/stepinside does) cannot build on Windows.

`bin.ts` hands `runCli` the working directory with its backslashes turned into slashes, `D:/stepinside`. `resolvePath` in `src/cli/run.ts` joins it with the argument, normalizes the segments and always returns `/${parts.join('/')}`, so the path becomes `/D:/stepinside/src`. On Windows that is not the directory: `fs.statSync('/D:/stepinside/src')` resolves against the current drive's root, finds nothing, and `host.kind` answers `undefined`. An absolute argument (`D:/stepinside/src` or `D:\stepinside\src`) takes the same route, since only a leading `/` counts as absolute.

Seen at e961248 (the pin in typeshade/stepinside) with Bun 1.3.11 on Windows 11. `main` at 035400fe has the same `resolvePath` and the same `cwd` handling. The Vite plugin is not affected; only the command line is.

## Expected

`tshc check src/` and `tshc sync src/` work from a Windows working directory, with a relative path, a `D:/...` path and a `D:\...` path, and print paths relative to the working directory as they do on POSIX.

One shape for the fix: `resolvePath` keeps a drive root (a first segment matching `/^[A-Za-z]:$/`) and returns `D:/...` without the leading slash, treats `X:/` and `X:\` as absolute, and `bin.ts` turns backslashes in the arguments into slashes as it already does for the working directory. `relativeTo` then works unchanged.

## Tests owed

`src/cli/run.test.ts` drives `runCli` through a fake host, so a case with `cwd: 'D:/work'` and a relative, a `D:/` and a `D:\` argument pins the fix without a Windows runner.

cases.title: The stepping debugger folds a kernel function's float reduction in loop order, not in Rule 7.2's tree
cases.body:
## What happens

A debug session over a kernel function returns a different sum than every tier computes. Measured on `main` at 41872ee:

```ts
"use typeshade";
export function total(xs: array<f32>): f32 {
  let s = 0.;
  for (const x of xs) {
    s += x;
  }
  return s;
}
```

With `xs = [1e8, 1, -1e8, 1]`, in f32:

| Walk | Result |
| --- | --- |
| `compileModule(m, { precision: 'f32' }).fns.total` | 2 |
| `compileModuleJs(m, { precision: 'f32' }).fns.total` | 2 |
| `startDebugSession(m, 'total', [xs])`, then `continue()` | 1 |

Every tier folds the reduction of a loop the proof accepts in the tree order:
- the oracle and the codegen (`execTreeFor` for a loop in `ctx.trees`, `src/core/oracle.ts:653`);
- the WebGPU plan (`kernel-lower.ts`);
- the CPU tier.

The tree pairs `1e8` with `-1e8` and `1` with `1`, which gives 2. The debug session runs the loop in iteration order. There, `1e8 + 1` rounds back to `1e8` in f32, so the sum comes out 1. Nothing under `src/core/debug/` reads `treeLoops` or `kernelTree`.

## Why it is a bug

- Rule 7.2's table (`docs/language-design.md:552`): "`s += x` in a loop of a kernel function the proof accepts: a fold in the tree order on every tier".
- Rule 8.22 (`:849`): "A variable an accepted loop reduces is combined in the tree order on every tier".
- `docs/debugging.md` §2.5 chose a second walk held by a differential gate: "A stepped run must return the same value as `compileModule`".

A developer who steps through `total` to see why it returns 2 is shown 1.

## How it was found

The generated-kernel differential of #349 has a stepping arm, S, which holds the session to the interpreter. It reported seeds 10 and 35 of `generateKernelModule`, in f64 mode with arrays of 5. Both kernels have a float reduction: a `vec4` product and a `vec2` sum. Example: `oracle [7.665376639300651, …] step [7.66537663930065, …]`, with the arrays equal.

Until this is fixed, the S arm compares only the arrays of a kernel whose accepted loop folds a float. An integer reduction is exact in any order, so S still compares its result.

## A direction

The session could fold as the oracle does: take the same `treeLoops(source, target)` map, and at a loop in it, step each iteration from the operator's identity, keep what each iteration leaves in the variable, fold those values with `kernelTree` when the loop ends, and combine the result with the variable's value before the loop. Each iteration would then show the variable as the GPU's invocation holds it, and the value after the loop would be the one every tier computes.

The fix's test is the case above, run through both walks: the session's result equals `compileModule`'s. The S arm of #349 then compares the result too.

cases.title: Determinism report: a textureGather on an integer texture is dropped, because DeterminismEntry.elem has no integer
cases.body:
Found while fixing the same class of bug for the four `pack` rows on `claude/lane-c-builtins-textures` (PR #164). That fix is in; this one is not, because closing it means widening a public type.

### What happens

`accuracyOf` returns the `filtered` row for any `textureGather*` id. That row is about **which four texels the footprint selects**, which is implementation-defined whatever the texture's element — so an integer gather belongs in the report exactly as much as a float one does.

It is not reported. `hitOf` takes a node's float kind from its result type, and a gather on a `texture_2d<u32>` answers `vec4<u32>`, so `floatElemOf` returns `undefined` and the node is dropped before `accuracyOf` is ever asked.

### Measured

Same program, three texture elements, `compile().determinism`:

```
texture_2d<f32>   [["textureGather","f32","filtered"]]
texture_2d<u32>   []
texture_2d<i32>   []
```

```ts
"use typeshade"
declare const tex: texture_2d<u32>
declare const smp: sampler
declare let out: storage<array<u32>>
@compute([1, 1, 1])
export function cs(@builtin("global_invocation_id") gid: vec3u): void {
  out[0] = textureGather(0, tex, smp, vec2(0.5, 0.5)).x
}
```

`textureGather` is the only filtered read this can reach: sampling is float-only on both targets, so no other `filtered` row has an integer result.

### Why it was not fixed with the packs

The packs were fixable inside the pass — a pack's float kind is the one it *reads*, so the walk takes it from the argument. A gather on an integer texture has **no float kind at all**. Reporting it means either lying about `elem` or widening it:

```ts
export interface DeterminismEntry {
  /** The float the operation computes in: native `f32`, or emulated `f64`. */
  readonly elem: 'f32' | 'f64'
```

`DeterminismEntry` is exported from the barrel, and widening a union in an output type breaks a consumer that switches exhaustively on it. That is a public-API decision, not a pass fix.

### Options

1. Widen `elem` to `'f32' | 'f64' | 'i32' | 'u32'` and document it as a breaking change to the report shape.
2. Add a separate, non-float field (say `elem: 'f32' | 'f64' | null` — also breaking) or a distinct row kind.
3. Leave it, and say in §38 that the report covers float operations, so a gather is listed only when its texels are floats.

Option 3 is the cheapest and may be the honest one — the report's own contract says "one row per operation **and float**" — but then §38 should say so, because today it reads as though every `filtered` operation is listed.

### Pinned in the tree

`src/core/passes/determinism.test.ts` carries an `it.fails` naming this issue, and `PACK_FLOAT_ARG`'s doc comment in `src/core/passes/determinism.ts` records the gap beside the fix that closed the pack half.

cases.title: compile() emits a constant expression Tint refuses: a divisor the optimizer folds to 0, and a module constant shifted into its sign bit
cases.body:
## What happens

Measured on `main` at e446235. Each program compiles with no diagnostic, and Tint (Chromium, SwiftShader) refuses the WGSL it emits:

| Source | Emitted | Tint |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `const x = data[0]; data[1] = 7 / (x - x);` (u32) | `data[1] = (7u / 0u);` | integer division by zero is invalid |
| `const x = data[0]; data[1] = 7 % (x ^ x);` (u32) | `data[1] = (7u % 0u);` | integer division by zero is invalid |
| `const x = data[0]; data[1] = x / (x * 0);` (i32) | `data[1] = (x / 0);` | integer division by zero is invalid |
| `const S: i32 = 3;` … `x + (S << 31)` | `(x + (S << 31u))` | shift left operation results in sign change |

(`data` is a `storage<array<u32 | i32>, "read_write">` read in a `@compute` entry.)

Each program is well defined in WGSL at run time: an integer `x / 0` is `x` and `x % 0` is `0`. The CPU oracle computes exactly that. What Tint refuses is the *constant* form, which WGSL evaluates when it creates the shader:
- a divisor that is a constant zero;
- a constant shift whose bits change the sign.

## Why

- **The divisor.** The front end refuses a constant divisor of zero with `TS8003` ("Division by zero: "z" is 0 on every invocation. WGSL refuses it"), and the four literal forms of these are all caught. `x - x`, `x ^ x` and `x * 0` are not constant to the front end. The optimizer then folds each to `0`, which leaves a constant zero divisor in the emitted text.
- **The shift.** `i32(3) << u32(31)` written with literals is folded to `-2147483648` and emitted as that literal. `S << 31` over a module `const` is emitted as written, and Tint evaluates it.

## Fix

- The fold should give an integer division by a folded zero WGSL's run-time answer: `a / 0` becomes `a`, and `a % 0` becomes `0`.
- A shift of constants should be folded like the literal form, or refused with the literal form's `TS8003`.

A test reads both halves on each source above: `compile()`'s diagnostics or emit, handed to Tint once (Rule 12.6, Rule 13.3), and the language service's diagnostics.

## How it was found

The GPU differential of #349 compiles generated programs on Tint. Seed 25 of `generateKernelModule(seed, { exact: true })` has `u32(3.14) / (g0 - g0)` in a helper, and the optimizer made it `(u32(3.141592653589793) / 0u)`. The generator's exact mode now keeps its own constant divisors nonzero and its constant shifts in range. It cannot keep the optimizer from making one, so the gate reports this until it is fixed.

cases.title: A `$` in an identifier compiles to WGSL that Tint refuses
Name TypeShade's spelling in the diagnostic when a shader uses a GLSL or HLSL name (`lerp` → `mix`)
cases.body:
Found while building the agent skill and MCP server in typeshade/vscode-typeshade#7. Measured on `main` at `0154222`.

## What happens

Models write GLSL and HLSL names first, and so do people coming from those languages. The compiler refuses the names, which is right. But the diagnostic's second sentence either points the wrong way or is missing:

| Source | Diagnostic today |
| --- | --- |
| `lerp(a, b, 0.5)` | `TS8004 Unknown function "lerp(a, b, 0.5)". Declare it in this file, or import it from another shader module.` |
| `fmod(a, 2.)` | `TS8004 Unknown function "fmod(a, 2.)". Declare it in this file, or import it from another shader module.` |
| `mul(m, v)` | `TS8004 Unknown function "mul(m, v)". Declare it in this file, or import it from another shader module.` |
| `a: float3` | `TS8002 Unknown type "float3". Supported names: f32, f64, i32, u32, bool, vec2, ...` (56 names) |
| `gl_FragCoord.x` | `TS8022 Unknown identifier "gl_FragCoord".` |

- For `lerp` the remedy "declare it in this file" is wrong: the author wants `mix`.
- `TS8004` quotes the whole call text, not the callee's name.

## Proposal

Keep refusing. When the unknown name is a known GLSL or HLSL one, make the second sentence name TypeShade's spelling:

| Source | Proposed |
| --- | --- |
| `lerp(a, b, 0.5)` | `TS8004 Unknown function "lerp". HLSL's lerp is mix here.` |
| `fmod(a, 2.)` | `TS8004 Unknown function "fmod". HLSL's fmod is the % operator here, which truncates like it.` |
| `mul(m, v)` | `TS8004 Unknown function "mul". HLSL's mul(a, b) is a * b here.` |
| `a: float3` | `TS8002 Unknown type "float3". HLSL's float3 is vec3 here.` |
| `gl_FragCoord.x` | `TS8022 Unknown identifier "gl_FragCoord". GLSL's gl_FragCoord is a parameter here: @builtin("position") pos: vec4.` |

- A name that is not a known foreign one keeps today's second sentence.
- `TS8004` quotes the callee's name, as `TS8002` and `TS8022` already quote theirs.

The table already exists: `FOREIGN_NAMES` in typeshade/vscode-typeshade, `packages/mcp-server/src/vocabulary.ts`. It maps 112 GLSL and HLSL names to functions, types, builtin values and attributes. Tests hold it to two invariants: every target is a name TypeShade declares, and no source is one. It would move into the compiler, exported beside the ambient library, so the compiler, the language service and the MCP server read one table.

## Why not aliases

Accepting `lerp` as a second spelling of `mix` was considered, and is not proposed:

- **The rules exclude it.** Under Rule 2.1 an author-facing name comes from WGSL, ECMAScript or §9.3's table, and `lerp` has none of the three. Rule 9.6 keeps §9.3 shrink-only, and "not a place to put a name that failed the source check".
- **Some names cannot be aliases without changing meaning.**
  - GLSL's `mod` floors, where HLSL's `fmod` and WGSL's `%` truncate. TypeShade's own `mod` is the floored one.
  - `tex2D(s, uv)` has a different argument shape from `textureSample(t, s, uv)`.
  - A wrong alias compiles in silence, while a refusal that names the right spelling costs one edit.
- **Two spellings of one builtin double what hover, completion and the docs have to show.**

## Rules

- **Rule 12.1**: the second sentence states the remedy, and for a foreign name the remedy is TypeShade's spelling, not a declaration.
- **Rule 12.5**: the message text is part of the contract. The refusal tests pin the new sentences, and `CHANGELOG.md` records them (Rule 13.8).
- **Rule 12.7**: one vocabulary. The table is data the compiler and the language service share, and each of its targets is checked against the ambient library.
- **Rules 2.1 and 9.6**: why this is a diagnostic and not an alias. No author-facing name is added.

## Tests

- The five rows above, each asserting the code and the full text.
- `myHelper(a)`, a name the table does not have, keeps today's sentence.
- The table's two invariants, against `SHADE_DTS`: every target is declared, and no source is declared. So `mod` and `saturate` can never enter the table and shadow a real name.
- A function the file declares named `lerp` still wins, with no diagnostic (Rule 9.5).

cases.title: A driver may reassociate f32 arithmetic (WGSL §15.7.5): an empty determinism report does not mean one answer
cases.body:
## What happens

Measured on Chromium's WebGPU (SwiftShader) in plain WGSL, with `x = 2.0` and `y = 0.001` (as `f32`) read from a storage buffer:

| WGSL | IEEE `f32`, as written | WebGPU |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `3.5 + (0.001 - x)` | 1.5010000467300415 | 1.500999927520752, which is `(3.5 + 0.001) - x` |
| `0.5 - ((x - 0.001) - 0.5)` | -0.9989999532699585 | -0.999000072479248 |
| `(x + 1e8) - 1e8` | 0 | 2 |
| `3.5 + (y - x)`, `0.5 - ((x - y) - 0.5)` | as written | as written |

Where a constant meets a constant across the operation between them, the implementation groups them together: it reassociates. With every operand computed at run time, this driver evaluates as written. WGSL §15.7.5 (Reassociation and Fusion) lets an implementation reassociate, and fuse where the result is no less accurate. Surface §38 already cites that section for the builtins WGSL defines by a formula (`inherited`).

## Why it matters

- **The report's claim.** Surface §38 says an empty `determinism` list "means every operation in the module has one answer, so a GPU result and the oracle can differ only by the oracle's own rounding, never by the driver's choice." Each `+`, `-` and `*` on `f32` is correctly rounded, and the report leaves them out. A chain of them, though, is a formula the driver may regroup. Under cancellation the difference has no bound: `(x + 1e8) - 1e8` is 0 or 2.
- **The GPU differential of #349** compares WebGPU with the `f32` oracle bit for bit where the report lists nothing, so its comparison rests on that claim. Over 200 generated kernel functions it meets two such chains, seeds 53 and 61, each 1 ULP apart. The 48 seeds it runs by default meet none, so the gate is green today by luck of the corpus.

## Proposal

1. **The report lists a chain.** A float `+`, `-` or `*` whose operand is another is a formula the driver may regroup. That holds through a `let` too, since the driver sees one value. The report lists it under a kind of its own, with no bound. A single operation stays unlisted, and §38's sentence is scoped to what is listed. This changes surface §38 and the report's table, so it needs a proposal.
2. **The GPU differential keeps its bit-for-bit claim** by generating float arithmetic that is exact whichever way the driver groups it. Literals and inputs become small dyadic numbers, so no intermediate value rounds. The harness checks that the `f32` oracle equals the `f64` oracle on each float it compares, which fails if a value was rounded. Division and the transcendental builtins are already outside the exact corpus.

(2) does not wait on (1): it takes rounding out of the corpus rather than trusting the report. (1) is the part an author reads.

## Recommendation

Both. I would do (2) in the GPU arm's pull request of #349, and draft (1) as a proposal for you to accept or change.

cases.title: Kernel proof: a row-major write whose width varies between iterations is accepted, and two invocations write one element
A hex literal containing the digit `e` or `E` types as `f32`, so every standard hash constant is unusable
cases.body:
## What happens

```ts
'use typeshade'
export function f(x: u32): u32 {
  return x * 0x9e3779b9
}
```

```
TS8003 Type mismatch: cannot * u32 and f32 — no implicit int/float conversion.
Cast explicitly: f32(intVal) or i32(floatVal) / u32(floatVal).
```

The literal is typed `f32`. It is a hexadecimal integer.

## Measured, on `main` (ae6b504)

Every literal below in the same program shape (`x * LIT` with `x: u32`): `0x9e3779b9` (the golden-ratio constant), `0x85ebca6b`, `0xc2b2ae35`, `0xdeadbeef`, `0xBEEF`, `0xE` and `0xe` all give TS8003. `0xff`, `0xabcd`, `0x1234567`, `0xFFFFFFFF`, `0b1011` and `1000000` are ok.

The rule is exactly "the literal's text contains `e` or `E`", which is the test for a decimal exponent marker (`1e9`) applied without excluding the `0x` prefix. `0xE` is the minimal reproducer.

## Why it matters more than it looks

Every widely used integer hash constant contains an `e`: `0x9e3779b9`, `0x85ebca6b`, `0xc2b2ae35`, `0x27d4eb2f`, `0x165667b1`, `0x9e3779b1`. So the whole family of integer hashes — murmur3's finalizer, xxhash, PCG's multipliers, Wang, the splitmix/lowbias mixers — cannot be written with its constants spelled the way every reference spells them. That family is what #181 replaces `fract(sin())` with, and it is what a noise or dithering author reaches for first.

The workaround is to write the decimal (`2654435769`), which compiles and emits correctly — so this is purely a lexing/typing defect, not a missing capability, and the emitted code is identical once the literal is accepted.

## Where

The classifier that decides whether a numeric literal is a float or an integer. The literal handling lives in `src/compiler/ts/lit-coerce.ts` and the lowering of a numeric literal in `src/compiler/ts/lower/expression*.ts`; the fix is to decide on the literal's *kind* (TypeScript's scanner already knows a hex literal is an integer — `ts.NumericLiteral` with a `0x` prefix, or `text.startsWith('0x')`) rather than on whether its text contains `e`.

Worth checking in the same change, since they share the classifier: a binary literal with no `e` (`0b1011`) is fine today, an octal (`0o17`), a numeric separator (`0xFF_FF`, `1_000_000`), and a BigInt-style suffix (`1n`, which should be refused with a sentence rather than typed).

## Rules

No rule moves and no name changes: Rule 5.1 already says what an integer-written literal types as, and this is the implementation disagreeing with it for one spelling. Rule 12.6 — a program the compiler accepts must compile on the target — is not the one at stake; this is the reverse, a program both targets accept that the front end refuses.

cases.title: GLSL: a module variable is emitted above the struct section, so a struct-typed top-level `let` names an undeclared type
WGSL's predeclared `matCxRf` aliases are missing, although the `vecNf` family is there
cases.body:
## What happens

```ts
'use typeshade'
export function f(m: mat2x2f): mat2x2f {
  return m
}
```

```
TS8002 Unknown type "mat2x2f". Supported names: f32, f64, i32, u32, bool, vec2, vec3, vec4,
vec2f, vec3f, vec4f, vec2u, vec3u, vec4u, vec2i, vec3i, vec4i, …
```

Measured on `main` (ae6b504) for `mat2x2f` and `mat3x3f`; the supported-name list the diagnostic prints shows the vector `f`/`u`/`i` aliases are all present.

## Why this is a gap and not a choice

WGSL predeclares the whole family — `mat2x2f`, `mat2x3f`, `mat2x4f`, `mat3x2f`, `mat3x3f`, `mat3x4f`, `mat4x2f`, `mat4x3f`, `mat4x4f`, plus the `h` variants under `enable f16` (Predeclared aliases). Rule 2.1(a) names "a predeclared type or type-generator including the predeclared `vecNf`/`vecNi`/`vecNu` aliases" as a source, and the surface already honours that for vectors. The matrices were simply not carried across when #166 made every `matCxR` a type.

So no §9.3 row is needed and no rule moves: these are WGSL's own names under Rule 2.1(a), and `docs/language-design.md`'s Appendix A row for matrices should name them alongside `matCxR` and the `mat2`/`mat3`/`mat4` short spellings.

## Where it bites

Rotation between fBm octaves is the standard cure for a lattice repeating, and it is written with a small matrix; the same for a Gerstner wave's direction turn and a curl-noise frame. An author following any WGSL reference writes `mat2x2f` and gets an unknown-type refusal whose supported-name list does not contain the name they were told to use.

## Scope

- Add the nine `matCxRf` aliases beside the existing `matCxR` names, in the same table (`SUPPORTED_TYPE_NAMES` / `src/compiler/ts/type-map.ts`) and in `SHADE_DTS`.
- The `matCxRh` family belongs with f16 (#153) and should not ride in.
- Check the same list for any other predeclared alias the vectors have and the matrices do not.
- `src/core/spec-conformance/surface-names.test.ts` sources these from the WGSL fixture, so they need no extension row — but confirm the fixture carries them rather than assuming it does, and if it does not, the fixture's bake is the thing to fix.

cases.title: Two struct declarations of one name compile with no diagnostic when the struct is unused
cases.body:
Found while reviewing `docs/language-design.md` (PR #163) against `main`: Rule 4.2 there cites `TS8023 DUPLICATE_SYMBOL` for a second declaration of one struct name, and the check runs only for a struct something uses.

## Reproduce (main `ee71d18`)

```ts
"use typeshade"

interface S { x: f32 }
class S { y: f32 }

export function f(): f32 { return 1. }
```

`compile()` reports no diagnostic and emits the module. Add `declare const u: uniform<S>` and the same pair is refused: `TS8023: Struct "S" is declared more than once. ...`.

Every case of `src/compiler/ts/type-structs.test.ts` that pins the duplicate rule declares a use of the struct (`const USE = 'declare const u: uniform<C>\n...'`), so the unused case is not covered.

## Expected

A duplicate struct name is refused whether or not the struct is used: the mistake is in the declarations, not in the use, and an author who later adds a use gets the error at a distance from its cause. One test row without a use.

## Design rule

Rule 4.2 of `docs/language-design.md` (PR #163); its Appendix B carries this row until the fix lands.

cases.title: A `return` with a value in a `void` function compiles with no error and emits invalid WGSL and GLSL
Two entries of one stage make `compile()` emit two `void main()` in that GLSL program, with no diagnostic
A constant vector shift amount of 32 or more compiles with no diagnostic
cases.body:
Follow-up to #71. The fix for #71 landed in a554778 (PR #80). It refuses a constant **scalar** shift amount outside 0 to 31 with TS8003 (`src/compiler/ts/shift-amount.test.ts`). A constant **vector** shift amount is not checked:

```ts
x << vec2u(32, 1)
```

This compiles with no diagnostic and emits `(x << vec2<u32>(32u, 1u))`. WGSL makes a const-expression shift amount of 32 or more a shader-creation error for each component, just as it does for the scalar case. Not yet confirmed through Tint.

Expected: the same TS8003 "A shift amount must be between 0 and 31", for any component of a constant vector amount that folds outside that range.

cases.title: CPU tier: a host call of a small shader function costs 50-75 times the same TypeScript
cases.body:
## Context

stepinside follows the rule "a shader function the host also needs is exported from the shader and imported by the host, so both run one piece of code". Its mesh shader exports `photoCell(q: vec3, k: vec4, grid: vec4): vec3` and `seenEmpty(depth, a, b, c, d, scale: f32): bool`: the fragment stage runs them for every fragment of a layer, and the host runs them on the CPU for every vertex of a layer, while moving it along its ray (a march and a bisection), up to a million calls per layer.

## What happens

Through the Vite plugin's CPU tier, one `photoCell` call plus one `seenEmpty` call takes about **3.0 µs** in Node 24 (vitest), against **0.04 to 0.06 µs** for the same two functions written by hand in TypeScript: 50 to 75 times slower. The measurement ran 300,000 pairs on fixed inputs, twice each, alternating, after warm-up.

In the product, switching the host from its own copy to the imported functions took the end-to-end test's layer from 295 ms to 895 ms; on a real photo, where a quarter of a layer's 100,000 cells are marched, it is seconds.

From reading `src/core/cpu-runtime.ts`, the tier emulates `f32` (`Math.fround` on each operation) and goes through generic helpers (`map1` and the like) for vector values, which is correct and presumably where the time goes.

## Expected

The CPU tier close enough to plain TypeScript that a host can call a shader function in a hot loop, which is what the "one piece of code" pattern asks of it. For example:

- a fast path for scalar and small-vector code that emits straight-line JavaScript (no per-operation dispatch),
- an opt-in `f64` mode for host calls where `f32` rounding is not the point, or
- documented costs, so a host knows to keep a copy for its hot loops.

## Tests owed

A benchmark of the CPU tier against hand-written TypeScript for a few representative helpers (scalar math, `vec3` construction and swizzles, branches), with a budget, so a regression shows.

## Pin

e961248 (stepinside's `vendor/typeshade`).

cases.title: CPU oracle: `compileModuleJs(m).dispatch` runs every entry on the interpreter, about 45 times slower than its own `fns` for an entry with no barrier
cases.body:
## What happens

`compileModuleJs(m).dispatch(entry, workgroups)` hands every entry to `dispatchCompute` on the interpreter (`src/core/cpu-codegen.ts:2014`), whether or not the entry has a barrier. For a compute entry with no `workgroupBarrier()` or `storageBarrier()`, calling the compiled entry once per invocation gives the same bindings and is far faster.

Measured on radiance's path tracer (`packages/kernels/src/trace.shade.ts`, a `@compute([64])` entry with no barrier, a `while`, storage reads and one `+=` into a `read_write` storage array), 8x8 pixels, 8 samples each (512 paths), `precision: 'f32'`:

| Call | Time per path |
| --- | --- |
| `cpu.dispatch('trace', 1)` | 6657 us |
| `for (i < 64) cpu.fns.trace([i, 0, 0])` | 147 us |

The two left the `accum` binding identical (`JSON.stringify` equal).

At M1's acceptance size (16x16 at 1024 spp), `dispatch` takes about 25 minutes and the per-invocation loop about 30 seconds. Radiance's oracle runner (`scripts/oracle.ts`) uses the loop, as the `CpuModule.dispatch` doc comment allows for a kernel with no barrier.

## Expected

`dispatch` on the JS backend runs a barrier-free entry through its compiled function, one invocation after another with the builtin parameters filled in, and keeps the interpreter for an entry that reaches a barrier. The two paths already agree, so a caller need not know which one is fast.

## Found by

typeshade/radiance M1 (the Cornell box, held to the oracle in CI). Pinned compiler e923a34.

## Tests owed

- A barrier-free entry dispatched through `compileModuleJs` gives the same bindings as through `compileModule`, and as a per-invocation `fns` loop.
- An entry with a barrier still runs in lockstep and still throws on a divergent barrier.
- A timing bound, or a counter, showing the compiled path is taken.
